advisor.summary: Above the §199A threshold ($403,500 MFJ / $201,750 single for 2026, with the OBBBA-widened phase-in), a non-SSTB's deduction is capped at the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of UBIA under §199A(b)(2)(B). When the wage prong binds, raising S-corp owner salary is counterintuitively accretive: each wage dollar cuts QBI by roughly $1.08 after employer FICA but lifts the cap by fifty cents, and the net deduction grows until the prongs cross near the classic two-sevenths wages-to-profit ratio. The same salary number carries reasonable-compensation exposure in the other direction — Watson is the standing reminder that the floor is enforced — so the target is set inside the defensible comp range, not just at the math optimum. The engine resets owner wages and prices the full interaction through the deterministic tables, modeling the 50% wage prong only; where UBIA is material, the alternative prong is computed off-model first.
mechanics: For taxable income past the threshold plus the phase-in range ($150,000 MFJ / $75,000 single from 2026), the deduction is the lesser of 20% of QBI and the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of UBIA — §199A(b)(2)(B) supplies the limitation this strategy tunes.

On the wage prong alone, the crossover sits where 20% of (profit minus wages and employer payroll tax) equals 50% of wages — roughly 27-29% of pre-wage profit; below that ratio, added salary grows the total deduction even as it shrinks QBI.

Each added wage dollar costs employer FICA under §3111 (6.2% to the Social Security wage base plus 1.45% Medicare, uncapped), and owner wages past $200,000/$250,000 pick up the 0.9% additional Medicare tax of §3101(b)(2) — the optimum is where marginal deduction value equals marginal payroll cost, so the model decides, not the heuristic.

Only W-2 wages properly allocable to QBI and timely reported count, computed under a Rev. Proc. 2019-11 method per Reg. §1.199A-2; partner guaranteed payments are not W-2 wages and cannot support the limit — this lever belongs to S corporations and entities with genuine employees.
Non-owner payroll counts too: accelerating a planned hire or year-end bonus raises the cap without adding owner-side Medicare drag.

The engine resets the S corporation's owner wages to the target and reprices the year end-to-end; it models the 50%-of-wages prong only, so capital-heavy businesses check the UBIA prong off-model before any salary change.

authority.note: The limitation: the greater of 50% of W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of UBIA of qualified property.
Determines W-2 wages (properly allocable to QBI, timely reported) and UBIA; guaranteed payments are excluded from the wage base.
The three permitted W-2 wage computation methods; the chosen method must tie to the W-3/941 filings.
The employer FICA cost of each added wage dollar and the 0.9% additional Medicare tax that steepens the marginal cost above $200k/$250k.

authority.cite: David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012)
authority.note: The reasonable-compensation floor: artificially low S-corp owner wages are recharacterized — the same salary number this strategy tunes upward is bounded below by this line of cases.
The IRS's foundational position that S corporation distributions can be recharacterized as wages for services actually rendered.
Made §199A permanent and widened the phase-in range for 2026 — the thresholds this optimization is calibrated against.

requirements: A non-SSTB S corporation (or an entity with common-law employees) whose deduction is actually wage-limited — verify which constraint binds before touching payroll.
Wages paid and reported within the calendar year on Forms W-2 and 941, tied to a Rev. Proc. 2019-11 computation.
A reasonable-compensation file supporting the chosen salary in both directions.
The UBIA prong screened off-model where the business holds substantial qualified property.
risks: Reasonable compensation is the two-sided audit theory: David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012) is the standing warning that artificially low owner wages get recharacterized — and a QBI-motivated salary set below the defensible range walks straight into it.
If the deduction is income-limited rather than wage-limited, added salary is pure payroll-tax cost; the constraint check comes first.
The engine ignores the UBIA prong; for capital-heavy businesses the 25%-plus-2.5% prong may already lift the cap, making added wages a dead cost.
Wages above the additional-Medicare thresholds steepen the marginal cost curve, and state payroll costs and salary-keyed benefit formulas move with the W-2.
An SSTB past the phase-in gets nothing regardless of wages — threshold management, not wage tuning, is the SSTB play.
stateNotes: Conformity: §199A is federal-only in most states, so the state effect of a wage change is payroll-tax and withholding mechanics rather than a deduction change.
PTET: shifting profit into wages shrinks the pass-through income base a PTET election taxes — re-run the PTET arithmetic at the new wage level rather than assuming last year's benefit.

Missouri: Missouri's business income deduction (RSMo §143.022) has no wage limit, so moving profit into wages shrinks the Missouri-side deduction base — a real, if modest, offset to price when Missouri is in the picture; SALT Parity PTET elections (RSMo §143.436) re-price at the new wage split.
reviewChecklist: Binding-constraint analysis in the file: 20% of QBI versus 50% of wages (and the UBIA prong where relevant).
Target salary sits inside the documented reasonable-compensation range.
Payroll change executed before December 31 with W-2/941 reporting confirmed.
Additional Medicare tax and state payroll costs included in the marginal math.
PTET arithmetic re-run at the new wage level.

client.teaser: The right salary number can unlock a bigger 20% deduction than the one you have now.
client.headline: Tune your own salary to unlock the full 20% deduction
plainEnglish: Business owners can deduct up to 20% of business profit. At higher incomes there is a catch: the deduction is capped by how much W-2 payroll the business pays.

Here is the surprise. If the cap is squeezing your deduction, paying yourself a somewhat larger salary can raise the cap faster than it shrinks the profit. Done right, the deduction grows even though salary went up.

There is a sweet spot. Too little salary and the cap chokes the deduction. Too much and payroll taxes eat the gain. We find the exact point for your numbers, check it against a fair-pay standard, and set payroll there.
client.analogy: Your payroll is the hand on a valve, and the deduction is the water flowing through. We open the valve to the exact point where the flow is strongest without wasting a drop.
benefits: A larger 20% deduction, often worth thousands each year
Uses a number you already control — no new spending
Doubles as support for your salary if the IRS ever asks
steps: WE test whether the cap is actually limiting your deduction.
WE calculate the salary level that nets you the most after payroll tax.
YOU approve the change; WE adjust payroll before year-end.
WE re-run the math every year as profit moves.
clientCommitments: Run the approved salary through real payroll before December 31
Keep us informed of profit swings so the target stays current

annualMaintenance: Annual re-solve of the wage target as profit and thresholds move
deliverables: Wage-optimization model with the marginal math
